definition: An attempt to apply an operation to a value of a type it isn't defined for, such as dividing a string or calling a number as if it were a function. Static checkers try to find these before the program runs; dynamic languages detect them as the operation executes.
example: In Python, "5" + 2 raises TypeError: can only concatenate str (not "int") to str.

definition: The set of rules a programming language uses to give every value and expression a type and to detect or prevent type errors. It decides which programs are accepted and which operations are allowed on which values.
example: Java's type system rejects assigning a String to an int variable at compile time.

definition: Checking types by analysing the source code before the program runs, usually at compile time. A statically typed language reports type errors without executing the code, though some run-time checks (casts, array bounds) remain.
example: Java, Rust, Haskell and TypeScript are statically typed: String s = 5; is rejected before the program ever runs.

definition: Typing in which operation rules depend on runtime value types, rather than requiring all operations to pass a static checker first. Implementations may use tags, specialise code or eliminate redundant checks; rebinding and single-assignment rules are separate language choices.
example: Python, JavaScript and Ruby are dynamically typed: add_one("41") fails only when that call runs.

definition: An informal spectrum describing how much a language converts mismatched values implicitly. "Strong" languages refuse most mixed operations; "weak" ones coerce freely. There is no single formal definition, so the labels are only rough.
example: JavaScript (weak-ish) evaluates "5" - 2 to 3; Python (strong-ish) raises TypeError for "5" + 2.

definition: An automatic, implicit conversion of a value from one type to another so that an operation can go ahead. How much a language coerces is what the strong/weak spectrum describes.
example: In JavaScript, "5" + 2 coerces the number 2 to the string "2" and gives "52".

definition: Writing the type of every variable and parameter explicitly in the source code, rather than letting the compiler infer it.
example: int count = 10; in Java is manifest; var count = 10; lets the compiler infer int.

definition: A type written explicitly in the source code next to a variable, parameter or return value, such as x: int. Depending on the language it is checked by the compiler, by a separate tool, or not at all at run time.
example: def f(x: int) -> int: annotates the parameter x and the return value as int.

definition: Python's name for type annotations (PEP 484). The interpreter stores them as metadata but does not enforce them; separate checkers such as mypy or Pyright use them.
example: def f(x: int) still accepts f("hi") at run time, but mypy reports the call.

definition: Extra information stored with a value at run time saying what type it is, so a dynamic language can check each operation. Optimising implementations may avoid some tag checks.
example: In CPython every object records its type, so type(3) returns int.

definition: Protection against the type errors excluded by a language’s stated rules and assumptions. Checked failures such as a Java bad-cast exception can preserve memory safety even when a source-language checker has an unsoundness; distinguish that runtime protection from a formal source-type soundness theorem.
example: A Java checked reference cast throws ClassCastException on an incompatible object instead of treating its bytes as the target class; this runtime protection is distinct from proving the whole source type system sound.

definition: Describes a program (or expression) that the type checker accepts: every part has a type consistent with the language's rules.
example: 1 + 2 is well-typed in Python's checkers; 1 + "a" is not.

definition: Robin Milner's 1978 summary of type soundness: a program that passes a sound type checker can never reach an undefined state at run time (Milner modelled this as never producing the special value "wrong"; later work calls it getting stuck). Controlled errors the language declares, such as a failed checked cast, don't count as going wrong.
example: An ML program that type-checks cannot add a string to a function at run time.

definition: Computer scientist associated with ML and the 1978 type-polymorphism paper introducing Algorithm W and the soundness slogan “well-typed programs cannot go wrong”.

A decision problem is undecidable when no algorithm always terminates with the correct yes/no answer for every instance. For a sufficiently expressive language, exact prediction of whether an arbitrary execution reaches a type error is one such problem.
example: No terminating checker can accept exactly the programs that never execute a type error.

definition: The question of whether a given program will eventually stop on a given input. Alan Turing proved in 1936 that no algorithm can answer it for every program, which is why exact type-error prediction is impossible.
example: Append a type error to arbitrary code P: deciding whether the error runs means deciding whether P halts.

definition: Rice’s theorem says that every non-trivial semantic property of partial computable functions is undecidable. Exact runtime error prediction in an expressive programming language can also be proved undecidable directly by reducing the halting problem; applying Rice’s theorem requires specifying how the error is represented in the semantics.
example: Run arbitrary code P and then perform a type-error operation: determining whether that operation is reached would determine whether P halts.

definition: A static checker that, unable to predict every run, errs on the safe side: it rejects some programs that would actually run correctly rather than risk accepting a bad one.
example: Java rejects Object o = "hi"; o.length(); even though o really holds a String.

definition: Converting a reference from a general type to a more specific type, such as Java Object to String. Java performs a runtime check when needed; TypeScript assertions and Python typing.cast instead provide no such enforcement. An upcast goes in the opposite direction.
example: (String) obj compiles in Java and throws ClassCastException at run time if obj is an Integer.

definition: An explicit instruction to treat a value as another type. Depending on the language it converts the value (3.9 to 3), checks it at run time (a Java reference cast), or just tells the checker to trust you (TypeScript as, Python cast).
example: In C, int x = (int)3.9; truncates to 3; in Java, (String) obj is checked at run time.

definition: A value used to reach data indirectly. Raw pointers expose address-like operations in C/C++; owning smart pointers such as unique_ptr, Box and Rc manage release under ownership rules, although leaks such as Rc reference cycles remain possible. Java and Python references are runtime-managed object references and need not expose a fixed machine address.
example: In C, float *f = (float *)&some_int; makes a float pointer to an int's bytes, and reading through it is undefined behaviour.

definition: The Java exception thrown when a checked reference cast fails at run time because the object is not an instance of the target class.
example: Object o = 42; String s = (String) o; throws ClassCastException.

definition: The Java exception thrown when code stores an object of the wrong type into a reference array, which Java must check because its arrays are covariant.
example: Object[] objs = new String[2]; objs[1] = 42; throws ArrayStoreException.

definition: C#'s equivalent of Java's ArrayStoreException: thrown when an element of the wrong type is stored into a covariant array.
example: object[] a = new string[1]; a[0] = 1; throws ArrayTypeMismatchException.

definition: Java ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException reports an array index outside its valid range; IndexOutOfBoundsException is the broader exception used by list operations as well. Other languages can reject, trap, return a missing value or have undefined behaviour for an out-of-bounds access.
example: int[] a = new int[3]; a[5] = 1; throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException.

definition: The Java exception thrown when code uses null where an object is required, such as calling a method on it.
example: String s = null; s.length(); throws NullPointerException.

definition: The Python exception raised when a sequence index is out of range.
example: [][0] raises IndexError: list index out of range.

definition: Python’s exception for invalid source syntax, raised when that source is parsed or compiled. This can happen before a module executes or later when running code calls compile, eval or exec.
example: An unguarded irrefutable capture followed by another case is rejected when that match source is compiled.

definition: Not a Number: an IEEE floating-point value used for invalid numeric results such as floating-point zero divided by zero. Its equality comparison is false even with itself; some languages raise an exception instead of returning NaN for a particular operation.
example: In JavaScript, 1 + undefined is NaN.

definition: Without a static type discipline in the sense relevant to a model or tool. In optional checking, unannotated code may be treated dynamically; assembly still has operand sizes and representation rules, so “untyped” does not mean every machine operation is meaningful.
example: An untyped Python function's parameters are treated as Any by mypy.

definition: Turning a value into its text form. In Java specifically, when one operand of + is a String, the other undergoes string conversion (primitives are formatted, objects use toString(), null becomes "null") and the two are concatenated.
example: "id-" + 42 is "id-42" in Java.

definition: Joining two sequences, such as strings, lists or tuples, end to end into a new one.
example: "ab" + "cd" concatenates to "abcd"; [1, 2] + [3] gives [1, 2, 3].

definition: A language-defined conversion to a wider numeric or static type. Java int-to-long preserves every int value, but int-to-float can lose precision; TypeScript literal widening instead changes a static literal type such as "hi" to the broader string type.
example: Java widens an int to a long silently; Rust refuses unless you write .into().

definition: Converting a number to an integer by discarding its fractional part, without rounding.
example: In C, int x = 3.9; stores 3.

definition: A language's ordering of number types (for example int, then float, then complex in Python) along which values can be widened when types are mixed.
example: Python's 1 + 2.5 widens the int up the tower and gives 3.5.

definition: Read–eval–print loop: an interactive prompt that reads one expression, evaluates it and prints the result, used for quick experiments.
example: Typing python3 with no arguments opens Python's REPL.

definition: A type checker that rechecks only the parts of a program affected by an edit, so feedback stays fast in large codebases.
example: mypy's daemon rechecks only the modules affected by a change.

term: To Type or Not to Type
aliases: To Type or Not to Type
definition: A 2017 study by Gao, Bird and Barr that took fixed bugs from public JavaScript projects and found TypeScript 2.0 and Flow 0.30 would each have detected about 15% of them.

Inferring types from a limited expression or scope rather than solving an entire program at once. Java var uses an initialiser; other languages also use context, later local uses or bidirectional rules. Annotation requirements differ across languages.
example: var n = names.size(); in Java infers n : int from the call's return type.

definition: TypeScript's name for inferring a type from where an expression is used, so type information flows inwards: a callback's parameter types come from the function it is passed to.
example: In [1, 2].map(x => x * 2), x is inferred as number because map is called on a number[].

definition: A type-checking approach combining inference of a type from an expression with checking an expression against an expected type. The expected type can supply information to nested expressions, such as a lambda’s parameter type; exact rules depend on the language.
example: Checking a lambda against an expected Function<String, Integer> tells the checker the lambda's parameter is a String.

definition: The expression that supplies a variable’s initial value at a declaration, such as 10 in Java var count = 10;. Type inference may use its type along with language-specific rules and context.
Java's empty type-argument list <>, as in new ArrayList<>(), asking the compiler to infer the type arguments from context.
example: List<String> xs = new ArrayList<>(); infers ArrayList<String>.

definition: A TypeScript type containing one literal value, such as "hi" or 42. A primitive const binding commonly retains its literal type while an unconstrained let binding widens it; properties of a mutable object can still widen even when the object binding uses const.
example: const c = "hi" has type "hi"; let l = "hi" has type string.

definition: An integer written directly in source code, such as 42 or 1u8 in Rust. Its type follows the language’s literal rules and context; an unconstrained Rust integer literal defaults to i32.
example: In let e = a + 1; with a: i32, the literal 1 is inferred as i32.

definition: Rust's ::<> syntax for supplying a generic function's type arguments explicitly at the call site.
example: "1 2".split(' ').map(|s| s.parse::<i32>().unwrap()).collect::<Vec<i32>>()

definition: mypy's temporary type for an empty collection whose element type isn't known yet, such as list[?] for x = []. A later use in the same scope, like x.append(1), completes it.
example: x = [] then x.append("a") makes x : list[str].

definition: A polymorphic type-system family associated with Hindley’s 1969 and Milner’s 1978 work. The HM core admits principal types using type variables, unification and let generalisation; languages such as Haskell and OCaml add restrictions and extensions, so the core theorem is not a claim about every program in those languages.
example: HM infers compose f g x = f (g x) as (b -> c) -> (a -> b) -> a -> c with no annotations.

definition: Milner's original inference algorithm for Hindley–Milner types. Luis Damas and Milner proved in 1982 that it always finds the principal type when one exists.
A placeholder standing for a type that is not yet known (during inference) or that callers may choose (in a generic or polymorphic type). Usually written a, b, t1 or T.
example: In first :: [a] -> Maybe a, a is a type variable.

definition: A condition that types must satisfy, such as "t2 must equal t3 → t4" collected during inference, or a requirement like Num a that a type variable belong to a type class.
example: Applying g to x produces the constraint t2 = t3 → t4.

definition: A mapping that replaces type variables with types, such as {a := Bool, b := Int}. Unification searches for one; applying it to a type rewrites every listed variable.
example: Applying {a := Int} to a → a gives Int → Int.

definition: In Hindley–Milner, turning the free type variables of a let-bound definition into "for all" variables, so each later use can pick its own types. Only variables not tied to the surrounding typing environment are generalised.
example: After inferring ident : t → t, HM generalises it to ∀t. t → t.

definition: The record of which variables are in scope and what type each has, usually written Γ (gamma) in papers, as in Γ ⊢ e : τ.
example: Inside a lambda, the environment records the parameter’s type; an addition constraint can restrict that type further. In Haskell, an unconstrained numeric literal alone does not force Int.

definition: The most general type admitted by a specified type system: every other admitted type is an instance obtained by substituting type variables. Algorithm W finds principal type schemes for typable HM-core expressions, with a given typing environment.
example: (b -> c) -> (a -> b) -> a -> c is principal for compose; (Int -> Bool) -> (String -> Int) -> String -> Bool is an instance.

definition: Marking a type variable with ∀ ("for all") so the type holds for every choice of it. ∀t. t → t means "for any type t, a function from t to t".
example: Haskell's id :: a -> a is implicitly forall a. a -> a.

definition: The step in unification that refuses to bind a type variable to a type containing that same variable, which would create an infinite type.
example: Trying to unify a with a function type containing a fails the occurs check; exact compiler diagnostic wording varies.

definition: A type that would have to contain itself, such as a = a → b, so writing it out never ends. Ordinary Hindley–Milner rejects it via the occurs check.
example: self_apply x = x x would need an infinite type.

definition: In the Hindley–Milner core, eligible type variables at let bindings are generalised when they are not free in the surrounding typing environment, so later uses can choose fresh instances. Ordinary lambda parameters retain one monomorphic type; practical languages add restrictions.
example: With standard Haskell instances, let ident x = x in (ident 1, ident True) type-checks; an ordinary parameter f in (f 1, f True) instead forces the unsupported Num Bool constraint.

definition: Types in which a "for all" appears inside an argument position, such as (∀a. a → a) → (Int, Bool): the function demands an argument that is itself polymorphic. Ordinary Hindley–Milner can't infer them; GHC supports them with RankNTypes and explicit signatures.
example: bad :: (forall a. a -> a) -> (Int, Bool) needs RankNTypes.

definition: The polymorphic lambda calculus (Girard 1972, Reynolds 1974), where types can be explicitly quantified anywhere. Full type inference for it is undecidable (Wells, 1994), which is why languages restrict where polymorphism may appear.

Deterministic exponential time: decision problems solvable with a number of steps bounded by an exponential in a polynomial of input length. ML typability is complete for this class; that is a worst-case statement, not a near-linear guarantee for real projects.
example: Nested lets that each pair the previous value double the type's size at every level.

definition: Generalised algebraic data type: a sum type whose constructors may return different instances of the type, letting pattern matches refine types. Powerful, but inference for them generally needs annotations.
example: data Expr a where IntE :: Int -> Expr Int; BoolE :: Bool -> Expr Bool

definition: Computing with types during static checking, for example with Haskell type families or TypeScript conditional types. Depending on the feature and restrictions, it can require annotations, complicate inference or make complete inference undecidable.
Haskell's type class for number types, providing +, -, * and conversion from integer literals. Num a => means "a must be a number type".
example: square x = x * x is inferred as Num a => a -> a.

definition: Haskell's type class for types whose values can be ordered and compared with <, > and compare. sort and maximum require it.
example: maximum :: Ord a => [a] -> a

definition: A GHC error raised when a type class constraint mentions a type variable that nothing in the program pins down, so the compiler can't choose an instance.
example: show . read fails: nothing says which type read should produce.

definition: A Haskell rule that stops some definitions without arguments or signatures from being generalised over type-class constraints, so they keep one type.

A declaration of a function's parameter and result types, such as area :: Double -> Double in Haskell or fn add(a: i32, b: i32) -> i32 in Rust. Rust requires them; in Haskell they are optional but idiomatic.
example: Adding area :: Double -> Double moves a type error to the function that caused it.

definition: The 2010 revision of the Haskell language standard, the baseline that GHC extensions build on.
A GHC flag that turns type errors into warnings and makes the offending code throw an exception when it runs.

The version of the lambda calculus in which every term has a type built from base types and function arrows. It rules out self-application such as x x, so it cannot express general recursion without a built-in operator.
example: x x is a valid untyped term but has no simple type.

definition: An untyped lambda-calculus term that makes recursion possible without named functions, built from self-application (x x). Simple type systems can't type it, so typed languages build recursion in.
How close a reported error is to the code that actually caused it. Inference can report a mistake far from its cause; explicit signatures improve locality.
A language feature that lets one definition (a function, class or type) work for many types through type parameters, while the checker still tracks the specific type used at each call.
example: List<String> and List<Integer> are two uses of the one generic List<T>.

definition: A placeholder type name, such as T in List<T> or first<T>, declared by a generic definition and filled in with a real type at each use.
example: In function first<T>(xs: T[]): T | undefined, T relates each input element type to the possible present result.

definition: The concrete type supplied for a type parameter at a particular use, such as String in List<String>.
example: In List<Integer>, Integer is the type argument.

definition: Generics whose type parameter is restricted to types supporting certain operations, such as T extends Comparable<T> in Java or T: PartialOrd in Rust, so the generic code may use those operations.
example: function longest<T extends { length: number }> accepts strings and arrays but not numbers.

definition: In Rust, a requirement that a type parameter implement a trait (a named set of methods), written T: PartialOrd + Copy. It is Rust's way of bounding generics.
example: fn largest<T: PartialOrd + Copy>(xs: &[T]) -> T

definition: Rust's trait for types whose values can be compared with <, > and so on, where some pairs may be incomparable (for example NaN among floats).
example: f64 implements PartialOrd but not the total-order trait Ord.

definition: Java's interface for types with a natural ordering, providing compareTo. Bounding a type parameter with T extends Comparable<T> lets generic code compare values.

A Python static-typing interface whose required members are checked structurally, subject to compatible signatures and member types. A class can satisfy a protocol without explicitly inheriting from it; merely having a method with the same name is not always sufficient.
example: A class satisfies an Ordered protocol only when its __lt__ signature is compatible with the protocol’s required comparison.

definition: Uniform behaviour across type choices, expressed by a relation-preservation theorem for a specified calculus. Total parametric functions cannot inspect an unknown element type; nontermination, effects, seq or unsafe inspection require their own caveats.
example: A total function of type a -> a must be the identity.

definition: Wadler’s parametricity method derives equations from polymorphic types under specified semantic assumptions. For a total parametric function on finite lists, rearranging elements commutes with applying a total element transformation.
example: For total parametric reverse on finite defined lists, mapping a total function before or after reversal yields the same list.

definition: A function returning its argument unchanged. Under total parametric semantics, a universally polymorphic function from an arbitrary type to that same type must be the identity; a concrete function from int to int has many other possible behaviours.
example: id 5 is 5; id "hi" is "hi".

definition: A function defined with a result for every input in its stated domain. For the total finite-value reasoning used here, it terminates without failure on every such input; specifying the domain matters. Parametricity for partial or lazy computations needs additional semantic conditions.
example: head is partial on finite lists because head [] fails; reverse is total on finite, fully defined lists.

definition: A computation that never finishes, such as an infinite loop. The simple totality arguments in this module exclude it; free theorems for partial or lazy computations require appropriately qualified relations and observations.

A list’s structure independently of element values, including its length and positions. A total parametric function from a finite list of an arbitrary element type to a list of that type can select, duplicate or rearrange existing elements without inspecting them.
example: reverse changes the order of positions but not the elements themselves.

definition: Checking generic types at compile time and then removing the type arguments from the compiled code, so at run time List<String> and List<Integer> are the same List. Java and TypeScript do this.
example: Java's f(List<String>) and f(List<Integer>) clash: both erase to f(List).

definition: A built-in value type that is not an object, such as int, long, double or boolean in Java. Java generics can't take primitives as type arguments.
example: List<int> is illegal in Java; List<Integer> is used instead.

definition: A Java generic class or interface used without its type arguments, such as plain List. Raw use loses some generic guarantees; particular calls, conversions or casts then produce unchecked warnings, rather than every declaration necessarily producing the same warning.
example: List names = new ArrayList(); is a raw type.

definition: A Java compiler warning that generic type safety can't be verified at some point, typically when raw types or unchecked casts are used.
The goal behind Java's 2004 choice of erasure: new generic code had to run on existing JVMs and work with old non-generic libraries without recompiling them.
In Java, a variable of a parameterised type referring to an object that is not of that type, made possible by raw types or unchecked casts. It surfaces later as an unexpected ClassCastException.

Specialising generic code for concrete type arguments, as Rust and C++ implementations commonly do. It enables concrete representation and direct operations but can increase compilation work and binary size; optimisers may merge, inline or discard instantiations.
example: largest::<i32> and largest::<f64> are distinct conceptual instantiations; this does not promise two separate emitted machine-code functions.

definition: A specific version of a generic or polymorphic definition with its type parameters filled in, such as largest::<i32>; or, in inference, a type obtained from a polymorphic one by substituting for its variables.
example: (Int -> Bool) -> (String -> Int) -> String -> Bool is an instantiation of compose's type.

definition: Growth in compiled program size, here from generating many specialised copies of generic code.

A Rust dynamically sized type accessed through a pointer such as &dyn Trait or Box<dyn Trait>, pairing data access with trait-method dispatch information. Dynamic dispatch can share caller code across concrete implementers, subject to optimisation and the surrounding generic code.
How Haskell typically implements type classes: a function with a constraint like Ord a takes an extra hidden argument, a record (dictionary) of the class's methods for that type.
example: maximum on a list of Ints receives the Ord Int dictionary and calls its compare.

definition: Creating code specialised for a concrete type or other known information so generic operations can become more direct. Whether it occurs automatically and which calls it removes depend on the compiler, optimisation settings and compilation mode.
Keeping generic type arguments available at run time, as .NET does, so code can ask what T is and store value types unboxed.
example: In C#, typeof(T) works inside a generic method.

definition: A type whose variables hold references to objects rather than the objects’ inline value representation, as in Java and .NET reference types. The usual .NET JIT strategy shares native generic code across compatible reference-type instantiations; exact strategies remain runtime-dependent.

In .NET, a type whose variables contain the value representation directly; copying a variable copies that value. The usual generic JIT strategy specialises value-type instantiations, but exact code sharing depends on the runtime and compilation mode.
example: List<int> stores int values without per-element boxing. The usual .NET JIT strategy specialises value-type instantiations; exact emitted-code sharing depends on runtime and compilation mode.

definition: Abstracting over type constructors, such as taking a parameter f that can later be applied to an element type. Haskell’s Functor f accepts constructors such as Maybe or []; Java, TypeScript and Rust do not expose the same direct Haskell-style constructor parameter, though encodings and other abstractions exist.
example: fmap :: (a -> b) -> f a -> f b works with f = Maybe or f = [].

definition: A Haskell type class for container-like type constructors that support fmap: applying a function to every value inside while keeping the structure.
example: fmap (+1) (Just 2) is Just 3.

definition: C++'s generics mechanism: code parameterised by types (or values) and instantiated for each set of arguments. Dependent parts are checked only when instantiated.
example: std::vector<int> and std::vector<double> are two instantiations of one template.

definition: Named compile-time requirements on C++ template arguments, added in C++20, giving clearer errors than unconstrained templates.
example: template<std::integral T> T f(T x); accepts only integer types.

definition: A Python typing object representing a type variable, traditionally declared with TypeVar("T") and optional variance flags. Python 3.12 introduced type-parameter syntax alongside that API; checkers infer variance for those class parameters under the typing specification.
example: T_co = TypeVar("T_co", covariant=True)

definition: The shared collection of type stubs for Python's standard library and popular packages, used by mypy, Pyright and other checkers.

Barbara Liskov's rule (1987; formalised with Jeannette Wing in 1994) that S should be a subtype of T only if any code written for T still behaves correctly when given an S. Checkers enforce the type part, not the behaviour.
example: A Square whose setWidth also changes its height breaks code that relies on Rectangle's independent sides.

definition: Subtyping that exists only where it is declared by name, through extends or implements. Two types with identical members are still unrelated unless declared so. Java, C# and Kotlin classes work this way.
example: class Dog extends Animal makes Dog <: Animal; a look-alike class does not qualify.

definition: Compatibility based on required members and their types rather than solely on a declared class name, subject to the language’s additional rules. TypeScript, Go interfaces and Python Protocols use structural checks; private/protected members, generic constraints and other rules can still matter.
example: A Robot class with name: string fits interface Named { name: string } without mentioning it.

definition: A named contract for members or methods that a type can provide. Java and C# classes declare implementation; TypeScript and Go can establish compatibility structurally when the required members and other language-specific conditions fit.
example: interface Named { name: string }

definition: A type that every other type (in its domain) is a subtype of, so it can hold any value but allows few operations without narrowing: Object for Java reference types, unknown in TypeScript, object in Python, Any? in Kotlin.
example: let u: unknown = 3; is fine, but u.foo is rejected until u is narrowed.

definition: An uninhabited type that is a subtype of every type in the relevant type domain, used for computations with no normal return value: TypeScript never, Kotlin/Scala Nothing and Python Never/NoReturn. Rust’s ! serves a similar practical role, but the Rust Reference specifies never-expression coercion to other types separately from subtyping.
example: After every union case is eliminated, TypeScript can narrow the remaining value to never.

definition: The rule for how subtyping between type arguments carries over to a generic type: if Dog <: Animal, is F<Dog> a subtype of F<Animal> (covariant), the reverse (contravariant), neither (invariant) or both (bivariant)?
example: Java's List<T> is invariant; Kotlin's read-only List<out E> is covariant.

definition: Variance in which a generic type keeps the subtyping direction of its argument: Dog <: Animal gives F<Dog> <: F<Animal>. Safe when F only produces (returns) T values.
example: A read-only Sequence[Dog] can be passed where Sequence[Animal] is expected.

definition: Variance in which a generic type reverses the subtyping direction: Dog <: Animal gives F<Animal> <: F<Dog>. Safe when F only consumes (takes in) T values, as function parameters do.
example: A handler for any Animal can be used where a Dog handler is expected.

definition: A generic parameter is invariant when changing its argument along a subtype relationship does not by itself establish either subtype direction for the constructed types. Freely aliased access that both reads and writes generally needs this restriction or another safeguard, such as runtime checks.
example: Java's List<Dog> is not a List<Animal>, so a Cat can't be added through an alias.

definition: A condition that must stay true throughout: a class invariant restricts an object's fields ("balance is never negative") and every method must preserve it; a loop invariant holds before and after every iteration; a garbage collector keeps a tri-colour invariant. In type systems the adjective has a separate meaning: an invariant generic type has no subtyping relation between its instances (see Invariance).
example: A bank account class with the invariant balance >= 0 must reject a withdrawal larger than the balance.

definition: Variance in which F<Dog> and F<Animal> are each a subtype of the other. Unsound in general; TypeScript still compares method-syntax parameters bivariantly for compatibility.
example: TypeScript accepts a Dog-only handler for a method declared to take an Animal.

definition: An object is aliased when it is reachable through multiple names or paths, so mutation through one path can be observed through another. Freely aliased read/write interfaces generally need invariance, runtime checks or another restriction to preserve type safety.
example: After const animals: Animal[] = dogs;, animals and dogs alias the same array.

definition: An array typing rule that preserves an element subtype relationship, allowing an array of a subtype to be viewed as an array of its supertype. Freely aliased mutation then needs another safeguard: Java and C# perform runtime store checks; TypeScript can permit a later type mismatch.
example: Object[] objs = new String[2]; objs[1] = 42; throws ArrayStoreException in Java.

definition: Choosing variance at each place a generic type is used, rather than once for the type. Java does this with wildcards such as List<? extends Animal>.
example: void printAll(List<? extends Animal> xs) accepts List<Dog> and List<Cat>.

definition: Declaring a type parameter's variance once, where the generic type is defined, as Kotlin's out T / in T, C#'s out/in or Scala's +T/-T. The compiler checks that T is only used in matching positions.
example: interface Source<out T> { fun next(): T }

definition: Java's ? in a type argument, meaning "some unknown type". ? extends T accepts any subtype of T (read from it); ? super T accepts any supertype (write T values into it).
example: List<? super Dog> dst = new ArrayList<Animal>(); lets you add Dogs.

definition: Joshua Bloch's mnemonic from Effective Java for Java wildcards: a parameter you read from (a producer) should use ? extends T; one you write into (a consumer) should use ? super T.
example: copy(List<? super T> dest, List<? extends T> src)

definition: In variance, a producer only hands out T values (safe to be covariant) and a consumer only takes them in (safe to be contravariant).
example: An iterator is a producer of T; a comparator is a consumer.

definition: A TypeScript compiler option (part of strict, added in 2.6) that checks parameters of function types contravariantly. Parameters of members declared with method syntax are exempt and stay bivariant.
example: With it on, (d: Dog) => void is not accepted where (x: Animal) => void is expected.

definition: TypeScript's umbrella compiler option that turns on a family of stricter checks, including noImplicitAny, strictNullChecks and strictFunctionTypes. It does not include noUncheckedIndexedAccess.
example: "compilerOptions": { "strict": true }

definition: In TypeScript, declaring a member as m(x: Dog): void (method syntax) rather than m: (x: Dog) => void (property syntax). Method-syntax parameters are checked bivariantly even under strictFunctionTypes.
A callback a program registers to run when something happens, such as a click. TypeScript keeps method parameters bivariant partly so DOM event handler interfaces stay usable.
A TypeScript technique that adds a fake marker property to a type so two structurally identical types (such as UserId and OrderId strings) can't be mixed.
example: type UserId = string & { __brand: "UserId" }

definition: Rust’s static lifetime on a reference means the referent can remain valid for the whole program run. A T: 'static bound instead means T contains no borrowed references with shorter lifetimes; it does not require that each value of T itself live forever.
example: let s: &'static str = "hi";

definition: In Rust, function and trait-object types that are generic over every lifetime, written for<'a> fn(&'a T). Rust's subtyping covers these as well as plain lifetimes.
example: for<'a> fn(&'a str) accepts a string reference of any lifetime.

definition: A Rust &mut T reference permits mutation with exclusive access to the borrowed location while that reference is used. Reborrows are permitted under the borrowing rules; the type is invariant in T so a write cannot replace a longer-lived referent with a shorter-lived one.
example: fn bump(x: &mut i32) { *x += 1; }

definition: A Rust type allowing a value to be changed through a shared reference (interior mutability). Because it permits writes, it is invariant in T.

Rust’s owning smart pointer Box<T>, commonly used for heap-allocated values and indirection in recursive types. Zero-sized values need no allocation; Box is covariant in T and mutation follows the borrowing rules.
example: enum Expr { Add(Box<Expr>, Box<Expr>), Num(i64) }

definition: Rust’s growable contiguous collection Vec<T>. Its struct contains bookkeeping and may own a heap allocation for elements; an empty Vec and zero-sized element types need not allocate. Vec is covariant in T, with mutation constrained by borrowing rules.
example: let mut v = Vec::new(); v.push(1u8); gives a Vec<u8>.

definition: An object-oriented language associated with design by contract. Eiffel permits covariant argument redefinition; its documentation describes resulting catcall risks and type-validity rules, so the guarantee depends on those rules and the implementation.

TypeScript’s readonly T[] view does not permit array mutation through that view. It can protect an API parameter from direct writes, but does not freeze the runtime array or prevent changes through another mutable alias.
example: function show(xs: readonly Animal[]) can't push into xs.

definition: Python's abstract read-only sequence type. Because it has no mutating methods, type checkers treat it as covariant, unlike list.
example: A list[Dog] can be passed to def show(xs: Sequence[Animal]).

definition: Short for algebraic data type: a type built from products ("this and that", like a struct) and sums ("this or that", like an enum with data), so the number of its values follows simple algebra.
example: A Shape that is a Circle with a radius or a Rect with a width and height is an ADT.

definition: A type holding several values at once, such as a tuple, struct or record. Its number of possible values is the product of its parts' counts.
example: A pair of bools has 2 × 2 = 4 values.

definition: A type whose value is exactly one of several alternatives, recording which one: also called a tagged union, variant or discriminated union. Its number of values is the sum of its alternatives' counts.
example: Rust's enum Shape { Circle { r: f64 }, Rect { w: f64, h: f64 } } is a sum type.

definition: The number of distinct values a type has, written |A|. Products multiply cardinalities; sums add them.
example: |bool| = 2 and |Option<bool>| = 3.

definition: One alternative of a sum type, used both to build values of that alternative and to match them. It may carry fields.
example: In data Shape = Circle Double | Rect Double Double, Circle and Rect are data constructors.

definition: A type with exactly one value, carrying no information: () in Rust and Haskell. Its cardinality is 1.
example: A function returning () returns no meaningful value.

definition: A type with no values at all, such as Rust's ! or an enum with no variants. Its cardinality is 0, and code typed to return it can never return normally.
example: A function returning ! must panic, loop or exit.

definition: One use of pattern matching: an expression that tests which alternative a value is and binds its fields in one step, trying its arms top to bottom.
example: match s { Shape::Circle { r } => ..., Shape::Rect { w, h } => ... }

definition: An extra boolean condition on a match arm, written if ... after the pattern; the arm applies only when the pattern matches and the condition is true.
example: (Cmd::Buy(n), true) if n > 0 => buy(n)

definition: One pattern => result branch of a match. Arms are tried top to bottom and the first that matches wins.

A match is non-exhaustive when some possible input has no applicable arm; an exhaustiveness check looks for those missing cases. Rust rejects a non-exhaustive match (E0004), GHC can warn with -Wall, and Java requires switch expressions and enhanced switch statements to be exhaustive under its coverage rules.
example: Rust rejects a match on Shape missing Triangle with error E0004.

definition: An unguarded fallback pattern such as _ => or default handles otherwise-unmatched values. It can make a match exhaustive, so a newly added variant can silently take that fallback instead of producing a missing-case diagnostic.
example: A _ => 0.0 arm makes area return 0 for a new Triangle instead of a compile error.

definition: A match arm that can never run because earlier arms already match every value it would match. Rust and GHC warn about it.
example: (Cmd::Buy(0), true) after (Cmd::Buy(_), _) is unreachable.

definition: The Rust compiler error code for a non-exhaustive match: "non-exhaustive patterns: ... not covered".
The Rust compiler error code for mismatched types, for example assigning an i32 to an i64 variable.
A compiler flag (in GHC, GCC and others) that turns on a broad set of warnings, including GHC's incomplete-pattern warnings.
example: ghc -Wall Main.hs

definition: A Java 21 pattern that matches a record and binds its components in one step, such as case Rect(double w, double h) inside a switch.
example: case Rect(double w, double h) -> w * h

definition: A Java switch that produces a value. With patterns over a sealed type it must be exhaustive, so no default is needed when every permitted subtype is handled.
example: return switch (s) { case Circle c -> ...; case Rect r -> ...; };

definition: The Java exception thrown when an exhaustive switch meets a value no case matches at run time, for example a new subtype from separately compiled code.
A type defined in terms of itself, such as an expression that may contain smaller expressions, or a tree whose nodes hold subtrees.
example: data Expr = Num Int | Add Expr Expr

definition: Reaching a value through a pointer or reference rather than storing it directly. A recursive Rust enum needs it (Box) so the type has a finite size.
A special reference meaning "no object". In Java every reference type silently includes it, so using one without checking can throw NullPointerException.
example: String s = null; is legal Java.

definition: Tony Hoare's 2009 description of his 1965 invention of the null reference, because of the errors and crashes it has caused since.
A sum type that makes absence explicit: a value is either None (absent) or Some(value). Rust calls it Option<T>, Haskell Maybe a. Code must handle None before using the value.
example: Option<String> is None or Some(s); you can't call len() on it without handling None.

definition: The type of value returned by a function or expression. Separately, Rust Result<T, E> is a success-or-failure sum type with Ok(T) and Err(E); a function can have that specific Result as its result type.
example: s.parse::<u16>() returns Result<u16, ParseIntError>.

definition: Rust's postfix ? on a Result or Option: it unwraps a success value, or returns the error (or None) from the enclosing function early.
example: let n = s.parse::<u16>()?;

definition: Extracting a success payload without supplying an ordinary fallback or propagating failure: Rust unwrap panics on None or Err, and Haskell fromJust fails on Nothing. Rust unwrap_or instead supplies a fallback and does not panic merely because the value is absent.
example: None.unwrap() panics with "called `Option::unwrap()` on a `None` value".

definition: Rust’s mechanism for reporting an unrecoverable failure. Depending on the panic strategy, it unwinds the current thread’s stack or aborts the process; message output and recovery also depend on runtime configuration.
example: Calling unwrap on None panics.

definition: Rust syntax that runs a block only if a value matches one pattern, binding its fields, e.g. if let Some(s) = name { ... }.
A TypeScript union of object types that share a field (the discriminant or tag) with a different literal type in each member. Checking the tag narrows the value to one member.
example: type Shape = { kind: "circle"; r: number } | { kind: "rect"; w: number; h: number }

definition: A checker refining a value's type within a branch after a test, such as typeof x === "string" or a check on a discriminant field.
example: Inside case "circle":, s narrows to the circle member, so s.r is allowed.

definition: Python’s typing.assert_never helper, available from Python 3.11. Checkers accept its argument only after narrowing to Never, exposing missing cases; if reached at runtime it raises AssertionError. A similarly named TypeScript assertNever helper must be defined by the application.
example: case _: assert_never(s)

definition: In Python's match, a bare name in a case: it matches any value and binds it to that name, rather than comparing with an existing variable of that name.
example: case RED: matches everything and rebinds RED; write case Color.RED: to compare.

definition: A pattern that matches every value in its relevant domain, such as Python’s bare capture name or underscore. Python permits an irrefutable case block only as the last case when it has no guard; a guard can allow later cases to remain reachable.

Design advice to represent only the domain states intended to be constructible under a type system’s rules. Runtime validation, unsafe escapes and structural extra properties still require separate consideration; a checked union alone does not validate external input.
example: A union of idle | live(sessionId) | failed(error) can't represent "live with an error".

definition: Engineer at the trading firm Jane Street, a prominent OCaml user, who popularised "make illegal states unrepresentable".
A trading firm known for writing most of its software in OCaml.
Alexis King's 2019 advice: turn raw input into a precise type once, at the boundary, so the rest of the program receives values whose type already guarantees validity.
example: Parse a string into a NonEmptyList once, instead of re-checking emptiness everywhere.

definition: Losing meaning by passing bare true/false values: process(true, false) says nothing about what the flags mean, while an enum like Mode::DryRun does.

Rust documents specific types for which Option has the same size, alignment and call ABI as its payload type, using an otherwise invalid representation for None. This includes thin references to sized values and Box with the global allocator; it is not a universal guarantee for all enum payloads.
example: On a target where &u8 is 8 bytes, Option<&u8> is also 8 bytes; Option<u32> has no corresponding universal byte-count promise.

definition: How a type's bytes are arranged in memory: its size, the order of fields and padding, and its alignment (the address multiple it must start at).

Rust's fixed-size number types: i = signed integer, u = unsigned integer, f = floating point, followed by the size in bits. i32 is a 32-bit signed integer; u8 an 8-bit unsigned one (0 to 255); f64 a 64-bit float.
example: let a: i32 = 5; let b: i64 = a.into();

definition: A Rust 32-bit unsigned integer type that can never be 0, so Option<NonZeroU32> can use 0 for None and stay 4 bytes.

Mixing typed and untyped code in one program, adding annotations a file or function at a time. A dynamic type (any, Any) lets the two kinds of code meet. Formalised by Jeremy Siek and Walid Taha in 2006.
example: TypeScript lets a .ts file call untyped JavaScript, with any at the boundary.

definition: A type system’s guarantee that accepted programs avoid the erroneous states excluded by a specified semantics and assumptions. Runtime checks, declared exceptions, unsafe code and implementation bugs must be accounted for; source-type soundness and runtime memory safety are different claims.
example: In TypeScript, const n: number = xs[0] on an empty array is accepted, yet n is undefined: an unsoundness.

definition: Completeness is relative to a specification: an inference algorithm can find every type admitted by its formal system. A different, semantic notion would accept every program that never executes a runtime type error; for sufficiently expressive languages no terminating checker can be both sound and complete in that latter sense.
example: Algorithm W is complete for HM typing rules; it does not accept every arbitrary program whose actual execution happens to avoid a type error.

definition: A case where a test or checker reports no problem although there is one. For a type checker, it is a real type error that goes unreported. Soundness means no false negatives; a false alarm (rejecting a correct program) is the opposite mistake.

The two theorems used to prove soundness. Progress: a well-typed program is either a finished value or can take another step. Preservation (also called subject reduction): taking a step keeps the program well-typed. Together they mean it never gets stuck. The style is due to Wright and Felleisen (1994).

In a specified operational semantics, an expression that is not a final value and has no applicable next-step rule. A language model can use such states to represent forbidden runtime errors; this is not automatically the same as C undefined behaviour or a deliberately defined exception.
The precise definition of what programs in a language mean, usually as rules for how each expression evaluates step by step.
A formal statement Γ ⊢ e : τ, read "in context Γ, expression e has type τ". Γ (gamma) lists the types of variables in scope; ⊢ (turnstile) means "proves".
example: ⊢ 1 + 2 : Int says the closed expression 1 + 2 has type Int.

definition: In gradual typing, the type representing missing static information, often written ? in papers and Any or any in practical tools. The formal dynamic type is consistent with every type; practical assignment rules can have exceptions such as TypeScript never.
example: let s: string = a; is accepted when a: any, whatever a holds.

definition: TypeScript's safe top type: any value can be assigned to it, but you must narrow it (typeof, a type guard) before using it in type-specific ways.
example: let u: unknown = 3; let t: string = u; is an error.

definition: A gradual-typing relation expressing that two types could agree where dynamic information is unknown. Concrete base types must match, while structured types compare their components; the dynamic type is consistent with every type. The relation is reflexive and symmetric but deliberately non-transitive.
example: number ~ ? and ? ~ string hold, but number ~ string does not.

definition: A relation R is transitive if A R B and B R C always give A R C. Subtyping is transitive; gradual consistency deliberately isn't.
example: Dog <: Animal and Animal <: Object give Dog <: Object.

definition: Computer scientist who, with Walid Taha, introduced gradual typing in 2006, and later (with others) the gradual guarantee in 2015.

A formal property relating programs that differ in type precision. Making types less precise preserves static acceptance and successful behaviour in the model; more precision may expose static or runtime type errors rather than arbitrarily changing a successful result.

A TypeScript construct (x as User, or y! for "not null") that tells the checker to treat a value as a given type without any run-time check. A wrong assertion is a common source of crashes in typed code.
example: JSON.parse(s) as User compiles whatever s contains.

definition: TypeScript's default of typing xs[i] as T rather than T | undefined, even though an index may be out of range. A known, deliberate unsoundness.
example: const n: number = ([] as number[])[0]; is accepted but n is undefined.

definition: A TypeScript option outside strict that includes undefined for potentially missing array or index-signature reads. Known declared properties and known valid tuple positions can retain precise types, so it does not add undefined to every indexed expression.
example: With it on, xs[0].toFixed() is an error until you check for undefined.

definition: A TypeScript option (part of strict) that reports an error wherever the checker would silently fall back to any, such as an unannotated parameter.
example: function f(x) { ... } errors: Parameter 'x' implicitly has an 'any' type.

definition: A TypeScript option (part of strict) that keeps null and undefined out of other types, so string | null must be checked before use.
example: function f(x: string | null) { return x.length; } is rejected.

definition: The Python proposal created in 2014 and implemented in Python 3.5 in 2015 that defined type-hint syntax and semantics for static checkers. The Python interpreter does not enforce the hints.
A mypy option (included in --strict) that type-checks the bodies of functions without annotations, which mypy skips by default.
A mypy option that reports an error for any function definition without full type annotations.
mypy's flag enabling a bundle of optional strictness checks, including --check-untyped-defs and --disallow-untyped-defs.
A Python function that tells the type checker to treat a value as a given type. It does nothing at run time: it just returns its argument.
example: n = cast(int, load()) checks nothing.

definition: A Python comment telling type checkers to suppress errors on that line.
example: x: int = "a"  # type: ignore

definition: A .pyi file declaring the types of a Python module's functions and classes without their code, used by checkers when the library itself has no annotations.
example: types-requests provides stubs for the requests library.

definition: Python’s typing.get_type_hints evaluates and resolves type annotations into a mapping. Libraries can inspect that mapping, but this function does not itself enforce arguments or results, and evaluating annotations can execute code.
Python libraries (beartype, typeguard) that read type hints and check function arguments and results when the code runs, raising an error on a mismatch.
A Python library that validates data against classes declared with type hints, converting or rejecting input when it is parsed.
example: For a model requiring email with no default, User.model_validate(payload) raises ValidationError when email is missing.

definition: A TypeScript schema library: you declare a schema once, and it both validates data at run time and provides the matching static type.
example: For a schema with a required string email, UserSchema.parse(payload) throws when email is missing.

definition: Checking input against a stated schema when it enters a program. The check establishes only what that schema and its configuration validate, not every business invariant or the correctness of an unchecked static assertion.
example: An API response parsed against a schema requiring email fails immediately when email is absent.

definition: Checks performed during program execution, such as validating a reference cast, an index or a boundary value. Sound gradual designs insert checks according to their semantics; optional tools such as TypeScript and mypy do not insert type-enforcement checks, although ordinary runtime operations retain their checks.
example: A deep Typed Racket contract can check that an untyped function returns an integer every time typed code calls it.

definition: Static checking that can be applied incrementally without adding runtime type-enforcement checks. TypeScript erases its type annotations; Python retains annotation metadata but mypy does not insert runtime enforcement.

A gradual-typing strategy using shallow shape checks at selected runtime uses rather than deep wrappers on every value. Reticulated Python and Typed Racket shallow mode use related designs; the exact soundness property and checks depend on the system.

Typed Racket’s default mode, enforcing typed/untyped boundaries with contracts. Immediate data can be checked on crossing; higher-order or mutable values use wrappers to check relevant later interactions, rather than deciding all future behaviour in one check.
A run-time wrapper around a value, typically a function, that checks each later use against a specification (for example, argument and result are integers) and reports which side broke it.
example: A function passed into typed code expecting (Integer -> Integer) is wrapped so each call is checked.

definition: Attributing a failed runtime contract to the side responsible for the violation, including later argument and result checks on higher-order values. Wadler and Findler’s theorem establishes excluded forms of blame for well-typed or more precise terms under its calculus and assumptions, rather than covering arbitrary runtime failures.
example: If an untyped function returns a string where Integer was promised, the error blames the untyped module.

definition: Wadler and Findler’s slogan for a theorem about a specified blame calculus: appropriately well-typed or more precisely typed code cannot receive the blame excluded by that theorem. This is not an unconditional claim about every possible contract system or runtime failure.

A 2016 POPL paper by Takikawa and colleagues measuring Typed Racket programs with every mix of typed and untyped modules; some mixes ran many times slower than either extreme because of boundary checks.
A program run to measure performance in a repeatable way.

A type-system discipline separating nullable and non-nullable types. Under a sound system’s assumptions a non-nullable value cannot be null; Dart 3 requires sound null safety, while other languages have their own interoperability and escape-hatch caveats.
example: In Dart, String s = null; is a compile error; String? s = null; is allowed.

definition: Rust code inside an unsafe block or function, where the programmer can dereference raw pointers and call unchecked operations. Bugs there can break the safety guarantees safe Rust relies on.
example: unsafe { *ptr = 5; }

definition: Haskell escape hatches: unsafeCoerce can convert representations without type checks, and unsafePerformIO permits IO to be presented through a pure-looking interface. Correct use requires additional representation and semantic obligations; their mere existence does not refute guarantees about the safe fragment.
Nada Amin and Ross Tate's 2016 paper "Java and Scala's Type Systems are Unsound", showing a program using null and wildcard bounds that compiles but assigns an Integer to a String variable.
The JVM component that checks class files before running them, rejecting bytecode that could misuse types or memory.
A TypeScript feature for splitting a codebase into smaller projects with their own settings, so strictness can be raised one part at a time.
A migration rule that lets type-checking strictness only increase: new files must meet the strict settings, and old files can't get worse.
example: New modules must pass disallow_untyped_defs; existing exemptions can only be removed.

definition: A tool that statically scans code for suspicious patterns or rule violations, such as new uses of any.

Short for TypeScript, a language adding static type checking to JavaScript-compatible source. Type annotations are erased from emitted JavaScript; certain language constructs such as enums can generate runtime code.

The languages descended from ML (Meta Language), created by Robin Milner in the 1970s: Standard ML, OCaml, F# and others. They share Hindley–Milner inference, algebraic data types and pattern matching.
Google's statically typed language, whose interfaces are satisfied structurally: any type with the right methods fits. It infers local types with :=.

A programming language widely used for server-side web applications. It uses runtime value types and specified coercions, with optional declarations and configuration affecting checks; Hack is a related language with its own type system.
Google's language for Flutter. Dart 2 made its type system sound with run-time checks on casts and covariant generics; Dart 3 enforces sound null safety.
Meta's gradually typed dialect of PHP.
A typed sister language of Racket (a Lisp dialect) that enforces types at boundaries with untyped Racket using contracts (deep mode) or cheaper checks (shallow mode).
A research gradual typing system for Python that uses transient checks.
Stripe's gradual static type checker for Ruby.
Meta's static type checker for JavaScript, similar in aim to TypeScript.
A static checker for Python typing annotations. Its default configuration skips the bodies of fully unannotated functions; --strict enables a version-dependent bundle of additional checks.
Microsoft's static type checker for Python, also used in VS Code's Pylance.
Meta's static type checker for Python.

Microsoft’s runtime and library platform used by languages including C# and F#. Generic type arguments remain available at runtime; native-code sharing and specialisation depend on the runtime and compilation mode.
An alternative Python implementation with a JIT compiler.
A file-hosting company that type-checked over 4 million lines of Python with mypy, adopted gradually.
TypeScript's dynamic type: assignable to and from almost every type and allowing any operation, so checking is effectively switched off for that value. Python's typing.Any plays the same role.
example: let a: any = 3; a.foo.bar(); compiles and crashes at run time.

definition: Base-16 notation, written with a 0x prefix; each digit stands for 4 bits. 0x41 is 65 in decimal.
example: 0x41 is the bit pattern 01000001, the code of the letter A.

definition: The raw sequence of 0s and 1s stored in memory. The same bit pattern can mean an integer, a character or part of an address; the type says which.

The usual name of the basic integer type, whose size depends on the language: a 32-bit signed integer in Java and C#; at least 16 bits (usually 32) in C; an arbitrary-precision integer in Python; and in Haskell (Int) a fixed-size machine integer of at least 30 bits, 64 on common platforms.
example: In Java, int x = 2147483647 + 1; wraps to -2147483648; in Python the same sum is just 2147483648.

definition: Bookkeeping stored with a heap object by a particular runtime, such as type, lock or identity-hash information. HotSpot header size depends on target, VM options and version; compact object headers became a product feature in JDK 25, but a universal per-object byte count should not be assumed.
Extra slots that a growable array (Java ArrayList, Rust Vec, Python list) has already allocated beyond its current number of elements, so appending doesn't have to reallocate every time.
example: An ArrayList holding 10 elements may have room for 16.

definition: A yes/no problem for which an algorithm always terminates with the correct answer on every valid input. Ordinary Hindley–Milner typability is decidable, although its worst-case cost can be high.

A relation that does not always allow two linked steps to be combined. In gradual typing, number can be consistent with the dynamic type and the dynamic type with string without number being consistent with string.
Using a value through a more general supertype, such as viewing a Java Dog reference as Animal. The conversion preserves the underlying object; it does not turn an Animal into a Dog.

A function not defined for every input in its stated input domain. In programming, nontermination or a failure such as taking the head of an empty list can make a function partial; specify the domain before calling a function total.

Information distinguishing which alternative a sum-type value represents, also called a discriminant. It may be an explicit field or encoded through a representation optimisation; not every enum needs a separate tag byte.

A specification of what code must accept, return or preserve. A behavioural contract can be a design obligation; a runtime contract checks specified interactions, such as a function’s arguments and results, and reports a violation.
A floating-point number written directly in code, such as 2.0 in Rust. Context can choose f32 or f64 in Rust; an unconstrained floating-point literal defaults to f64.

A named operation at the type level that forms a type, possibly from type arguments: Maybe applied to Int forms Maybe Int. A constructor can also take no arguments, such as Bool; abstracting over constructors is a separate higher-kinded capability.

A TypeScript member whose property value has a function type, such as m: (x: Dog) => void. Under strictFunctionTypes its parameters are checked contravariantly, unlike the exemption for m(x: Dog): void method syntax.
